t: Minimum Time to Revert Word to Initial State II
o: After t seconds, the first t·k characters are gone, so the word can only revert if the remaining suffix of length n − t·k already equals the prefix of the same length (the appended characters then rebuild the front). For "abacaba", k=3: at t=1 the suffix "baba" ≠ prefix "baba"? It does not match "aba"... checking t=1 fails, t=2 leaves "aba" which equals the prefix, so the answer is 2. If t·k ≥ n nothing of the original remains, so t = ⌈n/k⌉ always works. With n up to 10^6 we need an O(n) or O(n log n) string comparison structure — either rolling hashes or the Z-function — rather than comparing slices naively.
k: Word reverts at time t iff word[0 : n−tk] == word[tk : n]; if tk ≥ n it always reverts.
The answer is at most ⌈n/k⌉, so at most n/k candidate times need checking.
Z-array gives the check for free: z[tk] ≥ n − tk.

a.i: Precompute prefix hashes so any substring hash is O(1). For each candidate t compare the hash of the prefix of length n−tk with the hash of the suffix of the same length; verify character-by-character on a hash hit to eliminate collision risk.
s: Build prefix hash array h and powers p with a base and modulus.
For t = 1, 2, … while t·k < n, compare hash(word[0:m]) with hash(word[m:n]), m = n−t·k.
On a match, confirm with a direct slice comparison and return t.
If no smaller t works, return ⌈n/k⌉.
a.t: O(n) — one hash pass plus at most n/k verified comparisons, each O(m) but total verification is bounded by O(n) overall in expectation.
a.sp: O(n) for the hash and power arrays.

a.i: The Z-array stores, for each position i, the longest common prefix of word and word[i:]. The condition word[0:m] == word[m:n] is exactly z[m] ≥ m with m = n − t·k, giving a deterministic linear-time check with no hashing.
s: Compute the Z-array of word in O(n).
For each t with t·k < n, test z[t·k] ≥ n − t·k.
Return the first such t, otherwise ⌈n/k⌉.
a.t: O(n) — the Z-function is linear and the loop over t runs at most n/k times.

w: Prefer the Z-function in an interview: deterministic, no collision concerns, and it directly encodes the prefix–suffix condition. Pitfalls: forgetting the tk ≥ n fallback of ⌈n/k⌉, and using 32-bit overflow-prone arithmetic in C++/Java (cast to 64-bit before multiplying). Follow-ups: what if only a prefix of length k must match (period detection), or if appends were restricted to the removed characters (then it becomes a pure rotation/period question solvable with the failure function).
